penalties_applied.name: requires_human_fulfillment
penalties_applied.reason: Building and maintaining a native Windows SDK/overlay that injects multi-language spell-check into WebView2 requires deep C++/Win32/COM engineering work per integration; each customer integration is a bespoke engagement, not an automated delivery.

penalties_applied.name: requires_synchronous_human
penalties_applied.reason: Enterprise ISV/SDK sales almost always involve a technical evaluation, procurement conversation, and integration support — not self-serve checkout.

rationale: The buyer is real and identifiable — Windows ISV engineering teams shipping multilingual desktop apps — and they clearly have budget for SDK tooling. However, the actual solution (a spell-check overlay or wrapper library for WebView2) requires deep native Windows/C++ development that is fundamentally outside what Claude + standard factory tooling can build or deliver; it is not a prompt + landing page + Stripe problem. Operational autonomy is near zero: each ISV integration needs hands-on technical support. The combination of a hard build requirement and a per-customer human touch makes this wrong for a solo non-technical factory.
solution_plan: This opportunity is not viable for the factory as described. Building a production-quality WebView2 spell-check SDK requires a native Windows C++/COM developer, not a Claude-based prompt pipeline. Even if the library could be built externally, selling and supporting it to enterprise ISVs involves technical evaluations, licensing negotiations, and per-customer integration help — all requiring a human engineer. A solo non-technical operator using this factory cannot realistically build, sell, or maintain this. Recommend dropping and watching for a future signal if Microsoft closes the API gap.
notes: Failing build_gates: buildability_with_ai (3 < 6 minimum), operational_autonomy (3 < 7 minimum). Total also falls below min_total_to_validate after penalties.
